extra.message: The Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded to a known string. Because it signs session cookies, an attacker who knows it can forge sessions (including flask-login's _user_id) and impersonate any user, including the admin, bypassing authentication.

The admin creation command defaults the password to 'admin' (and the login page advertises admin/admin). These well-known default credentials allow an attacker to authenticate as the admin user, bypassing access controls.

Passwords are stored as plaintext in the database (db.String column, no hashing). This is confirmed by the plaintext comparison at app/blueprints/login/views.py:17 and the plaintext update at app/blueprints/account_area/views.py:35. A database compromise would expose every user's credential in cleartext.

cwe: CWE-256: Plaintext Storage of a Password

extra.message: The User.serialize property includes the 'password' field, exposing the stored (plaintext) password to any caller that serializes a user (e.g., the API user listing at app/blueprints/api/views.py:72). Passwords must never be included in serialized/API output.

cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

extra.message: Flask DEBUG mode is enabled in the application config. The Werkzeug interactive debugger exposed in debug mode can be leveraged for remote code execution (via the debugger console/PIN) whenever the application is reachable over the network.

The application sets the 'X-XSS-Protection' response header to 0 (disabled) by default, disabling the browser's reflected-XSS filter and weakening client-side defenses on top of the existing template-level XSS sinks.

The 'next' query parameter is read from the request and passed directly to redirect() with no validation that it is a relative/same-origin URL. An attacker can craft /toggle_xss_protection/?next=https://evil.com to redirect victims to an arbitrary external site (open redirect / phishing).

cwe: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect')

extra.message: State-changing POST endpoints (change_password, change_email, send_feedback) and the login form accept POST requests with no CSRF token and no CSRF protection library (Flask-WTF is absent). An attacker can forge cross-site POST requests to change a victim's password/email or submit feedback on their behalf.
